what_its_for: Telavancin is an antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial skin infections and certain types of pneumonia (lung infections) caused by bacteria, including MRSA (a tough-to-treat type of staph bacteria). It works by stopping bacteria from building their outer protective wall, which kills them.
how_to_take: Telavancin is given through an IV (intravenous) line directly into your vein by a nurse or healthcare provider in a hospital or clinic setting. You cannot take this medicine at home by mouth. Each dose is given slowly over 60 minutes as an infusion. Do not rush or speed up the infusion on your own.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose based on your weight, kidney function, and the type of infection you have. The usual adult dose is 10 mg per kilogram of body weight, given once every 24 hours. Your doctor may adjust this dose if your kidneys are not working well. Treatment usually lasts 7 to 21 days depending on your infection.
missed_dose: Because this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a medical setting, a missed dose is uncommon. However, if you miss a scheduled infusion appointment, contact your doctor or clinic right away to reschedule as soon as possible. Do not try to double up on doses to make up for a missed one.
storage: Telavancin is stored and prepared by pharmacy or medical staff. The mixed (reconstituted) solution can be stored in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C) or at room temperature for a limited time. Do not freeze the mixed solution. Your healthcare team will handle all storage details.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medications you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, because telavancin can interact with many medicines. Avoid unprotected sex or pregnancy during treatment — telavancin can harm an unborn baby. Do not use if you are pregnant unless your doctor decides the benefits outweigh the risks. Avoid taking other medicines that can harm your kidneys without your doctor's knowledge. Do not stop your treatment early even if you feel better, as the infection may come back.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you experience: a rash, hives, or itching; swelling of your face, lips, or throat; trouble breathing; a fast or irregular heartbeat; dizziness or fainting; redness, flushing, or tingling during the infusion (this may be a 'Red Man Syndrome' reaction — tell your nurse immediately); decreased urination or swelling in your legs (signs of kidney problems); severe diarrhea that is watery or bloody (which can happen days to weeks after treatment); or chest pain or pounding heartbeat.
when_it_works: You may start to feel better within a few days of starting treatment, but it is very important to complete the full course of antibiotics your doctor prescribed. Do not stop treatment early just because you feel better. Your doctor will monitor your progress with lab tests and check-ins during treatment.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Telavancin can cause harm to an unborn baby and should be avoided during pregnancy unless absolutely necessary. A pregnancy test is usually done before starting treatment in women who can become pregnant. Use effective birth control during treatment. Breastfeeding: It is not known if telavancin passes into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before breastfeeding. Kidney problems: Your dose will likely be lowered if your kidneys are not working well. Your kidney function will be checked regularly during treatment. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to kidney-related side effects and will be monitored closely. Children: Safety in children has not been fully established; use is determined by your child's doctor.
